findings.reason: The protected Python solution uses two pointers starting at p and q. When a pointer reaches None (above the root), it is redirected to start at the other node. They meet after traversing at most h steps at their lowest common ancestor. The two-pointer list-intersection technique runs in O(h) time and O(1) auxiliary space, making it concise, optimal, and interview-standard; no candidate is required.

Because parent traversal forms a singly linked list ending at None, redirecting each pointer to the other starting node ensures both pointers cover equal total lengths (depth(p) + depth(q) - depth(LCA)). They meet exactly at the first common ancestor node object.

Each pointer traverses at most twice the path from a node to the root, taking O(h) time where h is the tree height. Auxiliary space is O(1) as only two node pointers are stored. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts parent-linked Node objects p and q and returns the Node object representing their lowest common ancestor by identity.

The approach accurately details treating parent chains as linked lists, balancing path length offsets by redirection, and checking object identity. Alternatives and edge cases cover ancestor hash sets, depth alignment algorithms, repeated ancestor searches, ancestor-descendant inputs, sibling nodes, and root subtree intersections.
